title: AI in cybersecurity: Why adoption is outpacing trust
summary: AI in cybersecurity is everywhere, but trust in autonomous action lags. See what the adoption-trust gap means for IT teams and how to close it.
body_markdown:
AI in cybersecurity has gone mainstream, yet only about one in four organizations fully trust it to remediate threats autonomously, and the vast majority have made exceptions to their own security policies to accomodate AI tools. This post explains why adoption is outrunning trust, what that gap can cost organizations, and the practical governance steps that let confidence catch up with capability.


## The adoption-trust gap hiding in plain sight


AI in cybersecurity is now widely adopted, but very few teams trust it to act without human oversight. That tension sits at the center of how organizations are currently operating their security programs.


The tools are in place. Detection engines flag threats, automated playbooks trigger responses, and AI assistants summarize alerts that used to take analysts hours to sift through. What hasn’t arrived at the same speed is confidence. Most teams still want a person in the loop before an AI system takes a consequential action.


Research from the AI Fog Report maps this out across three findings. Adoption is high. Trust in autonomy is low and organizations are making exceptions to policies designed to keep AI deployments safe. Each finding in isolation may appear manageable. Together, they reveal a significant and growing governance risk. Each of these on its own appears manageable. Together, they describe a real and growing risk.


## AI in cybersecurity: how fast adoption is moving


Adoption has moved from experiment to expectation. According to the AI Fog Report™, 81% of organizations have meaningfully increased their use of AI-powered security tools, indicating that these capabilities are no longer limited to pilot projects sitting off on the side.


That shift makes sense. Security teams are outnumbered, alert volumes keep climbing, and attackers are using AI to move faster and probe more targets. AI for cybersecurity helps close that gap. It correlates signals across endpoints, networks, identities, and cloud, identifies patterns a stretched team might miss, and drafts remediation steps in seconds instead of hours.


For MSPs and internal IT teams alike, the appeal is the same: do more with the people you already have. AI-powered security solutions handle the repetitive triage so analysts can focus on the threats that genuinely need human judgment. The technology has earned its place in the stack because it solves a real staffing and speed problem, not because it was fashionable.


## Why organizations draw the line at autonomous AI


Fewer than one in four organizations fully trust AI to remediate threats autonomously. The AI Fog Report™ puts the figure at 24.5%. By comparison, 81% of organizations report meaningfully increasing their use of AI-powered security tools over the past year, highlighting a significant gap between growing AI adoption and trust in autonomous action.


The disconnect isn’t irrational. It reflects a real understanding of which tasks AI can perform reliably and which still require human oversight. One useful way to think about the distinction is through the lens of governance, explainability, and control. Generative AI is probabilistic. It excels at interpreting and summarizing large datasets, translating technical findings into plain language, and drafting a remediation script. But its outputs need validation before they are used to inform a high-stakes decision. Deterministic AI works differently, operating inside strict logic paths that produce predictable, repeatable results, which makes it better suited to controlled validation and action.


The smart approach uses both. Generative AI proposes a remediation script; deterministic AI checks that script against safety policies before anything runs, helping prevent an automated fix from crashing a critical server or blocking legitimate traffic. Teams that hesitate to hand over full autonomy usually aren’t afraid of AI. They’ve simply recognized that an incorrect action in security can have real operational consequences, and they want to understand what happened, why it happened, and how to correct it.


This isn’t just a cybersecurity quirk. McKinsey’s[2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/tech-forward/state-of-ai-trust-in-2026-shifting-to-the-agentic-era) found that security and risk concerns are the top barrier to fully scaling autonomous AI across industries, cited by nearly two-thirds of respondents. The trust gap is broad, and it grows as systems take on more independent actions.


## The hidden cost of AI governance shortcuts


The real risk isn’t slow adoption. It’s the shortcuts teams take to speed it up. The AI Fog Report found that 87.1% of organizations have made at least minor exceptions to their own security policies to enable AI tools.


Consider that number. Nearly nine in 10 organizations have made exceptions to policies designed to protect them just to get AI capabilities working. This is how deployment quietly outruns oversight. A tool needs broader data access than existing policy allows, so an exception is granted. An assistant needs to reach a system it shouldn’t, so a control gets relaxed. Each decision looks small in isolation. Taken together, they add up to a security posture that no one actually designed.


The problem gets worse when you can’t see which tools you’ve accumulated. Only 51.9% of organizations maintain a comprehensive inventory of their AI tools. You can’t govern what you can’t see, and untracked AI creates both compliance gaps and security blind spots. Unsanctioned tools can move sensitive data to unvetted models, potentially leaving no record of what was shared. This is exactly the exposure that[Shadow AI Visibility](https://www.n-able.com/resources/adlumin-shadow-ai-visibility) addresses. It uses network telemetry already in your environment to inventory every active AI tool, attribute usage to specific users and machines, and produce audit-grade evidence for frameworks including SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, and GDPR.


## What organizations need before trust can catch up with adoption


Closing the adoption-trust gap comes down to four practical governance capabilities that make AI actions understandable, auditable, and controlled. Build these in from the start rather than retrofitting them after an incident.


- **Explainability.** Every AI-enabled action should answer three questions: what happened, why it happened, and how to inspect or correct it. If a decision cannot be explained, it cannot be trusted or justified, and it cannot be defended to an auditor or client.
- **Auditability.** Keep a durable, searchable record of AI interactions and the policies that governed them. Detection without context creates noise. Detection enriched with context and supported by an audit trail enriched with context and supported by an audit trail creates actionable intelligence.
- **Defined human-approval points.** Decide in advance which actions AI can take on its own and which require a human to sign off. Higher-risk decisions with real operational or business consequences should remain under human control.
- **A phased approach to automation.** Trust is earned in stages, not granted all at once. Move from AI that recommends, to AI that acts under supervision, to broader autonomy only where you have proven the guardrails hold. This crawl- walk-run progression is how confidence catches up with capability.


Grounding these steps in a recognized standard helps. The[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) offers a vendor-neutral structure for building trustworthiness into AI systems through its Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions. Anchoring your internal governance to a framework like this gives auditors, insurers, and clients a shared reference point, and it turns AI trust from a compliance chore into a business enabler. McKinsey found that organizations with clear, explicit accountability for responsible AI score materially higher on maturity than those without it.

The practical answer to the trust gap is human-supervised automation, not blind autonomy. Organizations don’t have to choose between the speed of AI and the confidence of human oversight. The most effective security operations combine both.

They provide** fully contextualized incidents with evidence and recommended actions rather than raw alerts. **Because your team works in the same system as the SOC, you can see how alerts are triaged, which actions have been taken, and what remains under investigation. That transparency helps make the automation trustworthy.** This is the model behind[Adlumin MDR](https://www.n-able.com/products/adlumin/mdr) . The same logic applies to endpoint management.[Unified endpoint management](https://www.n-able.com/solutions/unified-endpoint-management) brings AI-assisted vulnerability and patch management, automated hardening, and real-time endpoint visibility together with the controls needed to manage and secure your entire endpoint estate. That combination reduces response time and analyst workload without asking you to trust a black box. It gives you the speed AI promises and the visibility governance requires.


## Let trust catch up with capability


The numbers tell a clear story. Adoption of AI in cybersecurity has raced ahead, trust in full autonomy has lagged behind, and too many teams are closing the gap with policy exceptions instead of governance. That approach may accelerate deployment in the short term, but it creates longer-term security and compliance risks. The organizations that will get the most from AI are the ones treating trust as a capability to build, through explainability, auditability, clear human-approval points, and phased automation, rather than a hurdle to overcome.
